lesson.title: The Solution Region: Where All the Shading Overlaps
lesson.summary: The solution region of a system of inequalities is the complete set of points satisfying every inequality at once, the area where all the individual shadings overlap, and it can be bounded or unbounded, with edges included or excluded.
lesson.body:
After graphing a system of inequalities and shading each individual half-plane, the solution region is precisely the area where all of those shadings overlap: every ordered pair lying inside that overlap satisfies every inequality in the system at the same time. Unlike the single point that solves a typical system of equations, the solution region of a system of inequalities usually contains infinitely many ordered pairs, spread across a two-dimensional area of the plane rather than concentrated at one location. The solution region is, in effect, the final picture that all the earlier boundary-drawing and shading steps were building toward.

Whether a boundary edge actually belongs to the solution region depends on the same solid-versus-dashed distinction used while graphing. Edges drawn as solid lines, coming from inequalities with less than or equal to or greater than or equal to, are included in the region, so points exactly on those edges do count as solutions. Edges drawn as dashed lines, coming from strict inequalities, are not included, so points exactly on those edges are excluded even though points arbitrarily close to them, on the shaded side, are solutions. A region can even mix solid and dashed edges within the same system, so each boundary must be checked on its own rather than assuming the whole region behaves the same way along every edge.

Consider the system x >= 0, y >= 0, and x + y <= 4. All three inequalities include equality, so every boundary line is solid: the y-axis, from x >= 0, the x-axis, from y >= 0, and the line x + y = 4. These three lines meet each other at three points, forming a triangular region with corners at (0, 0), (4, 0), and (0, 4).

Checking the corners confirms the region. At (0, 0): 0 >= 0 is true, 0 >= 0 is true, and 0 + 0 = 0 <= 4 is true, so all three inequalities hold. At (4, 0): 4 >= 0 is true, 0 >= 0 is true, and 4 + 0 = 4 <= 4 is true, so all three hold. At (0, 4): 0 >= 0 is true, 4 >= 0 is true, and 0 + 4 = 4 <= 4 is true, so all three hold again. Since all three corners, along with every point inside the triangle they form, satisfy all three inequalities simultaneously, the bounded triangular region with those corners is the solution region of this system, and because every boundary is solid, the edges of the triangle themselves are part of the solution as well.

Not every solution region closes up into a bounded shape like this triangle. A system built from only two inequalities, or from inequalities that open in the same general direction rather than pinching inward like this one, can produce an unbounded region stretching out forever in some direction. Because a region's overall shape can vary so much, testing a specific point, exactly as done throughout these examples, remains the most dependable way to confirm whether it truly belongs to a system's solution region, regardless of whether that region turns out to be a bounded polygon or an unbounded strip.
